Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette: Margaret's world had been forever altered on that fateful evening two years ago. Her husband of thirty-five years, John, had been struck and killed by a car while walking home from work. The pain still felt like an open wound, refusing to heal with time. As the anniversary of his passing approached, Margaret found herself becoming increasingly anxious, as if the very date itself was a ticking time bomb waiting to unleash a torrent of emotions. On quiet evenings, when the house creaked and groaned around her, Margaret would startle at the slightest unexpected movement nearby, her heart racing as if she were in imminent danger. She couldn't shake the feeling that something terrible was lurking just out of sight, waiting to strike again. The sound of ambulances or the sight of cars involved in accidents sent her spiraling into a vortex of fear and dread. It was as if these triggers had become hardwired into her nervous system, primed to respond at a moment's notice. But it wasn't just external stimuli that set Margaret on edge – her memories of that fateful night also lingered, potent and unsettling. When she closed her eyes, she could almost smell the sweet scent of blooming flowers that had been present in the hospital where John was pronounced dead. These olfactory recollections would often transport her back to that moment, making it feel as if no time had passed at all. The memory itself remained stubbornly elusive, however – whenever Margaret tried to deliberately recall the events leading up to John's death, she found herself struggling to access the details. As a result, the memories would often resurface without warning, triggered by something in her surroundings that seemed innocuous enough to anyone else. A car driving down the street might suddenly bring back the full force of that terrible night, and Margaret would be left reeling once more. This unpredictability made it difficult for her to feel safe or in control – every moment felt like a potential minefield waiting to be detonated. In response, Margaret had developed an elaborate system of door and lock checking, methodically verifying that each entrance point to her home was secure multiple times throughout the day. It was a small measure of control in a world that seemed determined to undermine her at every turn. As night began to fall, she would lie awake for hours, listening intently for any sign of movement outside – the creaks and groans of the house taking on sinister proportions as the darkness deepened. Margaret knew intellectually that these rituals were unlikely to prevent another tragedy from occurring, but they had become an essential part of her coping mechanism. She couldn't help feeling that if only she could prepare for every eventuality, she might somehow ward off the darkness that seemed determined to consume her. It was this unending cycle of fear and hypervigilance that had finally brought Margaret to seek professional help – a sense of desperation creeping in as she realized she couldn't keep living like this. What she hoped for most now was to find some semblance of peace, a way to lay the memories of that terrible night to rest without surrendering to the crushing weight of her own fear.
